Chapter 2: Life in Africa Before the Disruption of Slavery
Before ships ever set sail for distant shores, West Africa was alive with tradition, community, and deep meaning. Picture a village nestled among forests and rivers, where a young boy wakes each morning to the sounds of drums, children’s laughter, and the gentle wisdom of elders.
In this place, everyone had a part to play. Kids learned side by side with their parents and grandparents, soaking up lessons on respect, responsibility, and what it means to belong. The boy’s father was known throughout the village for his strength and his fairness. His mother wove stories and songs right into their daily routines, making each day feel special. The boy watched, listened, and couldn’t wait for the day he’d step into the world of the grown-ups.
Growing up wasn’t just about getting older; it was celebrated. Rites of passage—special ceremonies—helped boys and girls prove their courage and learn the values of their people. These moments were about more than just the individual. They were about joining a community that shared a rich history and a sense of purpose.
Even though the village felt close-knit, it wasn’t cut off from the world. Traders and travelers brought news from far away, sparking everyone’s curiosity about lands beyond the horizon. Still, there was comfort in the familiar rhythm of daily life. The boy learned to hunt and fish, and he grew up respecting the spirits believed to watch over the land. At night, stories about ancestors were told around the fire, weaving the past into the present.
But all of that changed in an instant. When strangers arrived, the boy—now a young man—was captured and ripped away from everything he’d ever known. The violence was swift and brutal. He was bound, forced to march for days, and thrown onto a ship heading somewhere unimaginable. That journey across the ocean became a nightmare filled with fear, sickness, and despair.
Back home, the loss was unbearable. Families grieved for those who had vanished, not knowing if they’d ever return. The village’s sense of togetherness was shattered, but the memories of those taken—like the boy, his name, and his family—became part of the community’s story. These memories served as a reminder of what was lost, and of the strength that still remained.
Being ripped from home, from everything familiar, left wounds that ran deep. Yet, even in the darkest moments, the boy clung to the lessons of his childhood. The values his family taught him became his anchor. The memory of belonging—of home—was his lifeline in a world determined to erase his identity.
The story of life in Africa before slavery reminds us that those who were enslaved weren’t empty vessels. They came from vibrant communities, shaped by histories and traditions. The trauma they faced wasn’t just physical—it was an attack on memory, on identity, on everything that made them who they were. And yet, their resilience ran deep, fueled by stories and values carried across the sea.
